metaDescription: The best medicine balls under $50 for 2026: bouncing rubber, sand-filled slam and soft-shell balls from 6 to 20 lb, compared on shell, grip and the right use.
expertTake: The Amazon Basics 6 lb rubber medicine ball is our top pick under $50 because a firm, textured rubber shell that bounces suits core work, partner passes and wall throws for most people, and the Amazon Basics 15 lb slam ball is the value pick for slams and conditioning. A slam ball and a bouncing medicine ball are different tools, and using one for the other's job shortens its life. Anyone who wants a wall ball for high-rep throws or a soft shell for partner work should read the shell notes before buying.
introParagraphs: A medicine ball is a weighted ball you throw, slam, rotate and carry to build core strength, power and conditioning. It is one of the cheapest and most versatile pieces of home gym equipment, but the shell matters: a ball designed for slamming does not bounce, and a ball designed for bouncing is not meant to be slammed. A single ball and a few square feet of floor are enough to build a real routine.

Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when the guide was updated, so check the listing before you buy. We compare shell type, weight options, grip and the use each ball is built for, and we explain the difference between a slam ball and a medicine ball so you buy the right one.

products.name: Amazon Basics 6 lb Rubber Medicine Ball, 7.6 in, Textured Grip
products.description:
The Amazon Basics 6 lb medicine ball is a firm rubber ball 7.6 inches across, with a lightly textured surface for grip and the weight labeled on both sides. It is designed for core strength, balance and full-body workouts. The size and weight suit most adults.

Compared with the Retrospec soft ball, it bounces and is firmer, which suits wall throws and floor passes. Against the slam balls, it is a bouncing ball and should not be slammed hard. The textured surface grips well even with sweaty hands.

Start with a few slow rotations and presses, then add throws. Wipe the rubber clean after use. It suits beginners and people who want a general-purpose medicine ball. A simple starter routine is three sets of ten Russian twists, ten chest passes against a sturdy wall and eight overhead presses, resting a minute between sets. Because the weight is printed on both sides, you can read it at a glance while the ball is moving, which helps when you share it with a partner.
products.bestFor: Beginners and general fitness who want one versatile bouncing medicine ball.
pros: Firm rubber shell bounces and passes well

products.name: Retrospec Core Soft Medicine Ball, Vegan Leather, 4 to 30 lb Options
products.description:
The Retrospec Core ball has a soft vegan leather shell with a slip-resistant textured grip and is offered in ten weights from 4 to 30 lb. The soft shell is gentler on hands and floors than rubber. The range lets you start light and add weight as you build strength.

Compared with the Amazon Basics rubber ball, it is softer and less likely to sting when caught, but it does not bounce as well. Against the slam balls, it is meant for throws and passes rather than hard slams. The weight options make it the most progressive choice.

Wipe the shell with a damp cloth and keep it away from sharp objects. It suits partner work, wall throws and indoor training. The soft shell also makes it a good choice for seated and floor work, such as sit-up throws to a partner, where a hard ball would be uncomfortable. If you buy a lighter weight first, you can add a heavier one later and keep both for different drills in the same session.
products.bestFor: Partner work and indoor training where a soft shell and many weight options matter.
pros: Soft shell is gentler on hands
Good for partner passes and wall throws

products.name: Amazon Basics Heavy-Duty Slam Medicine Ball, 15 lb, Sand-Filled PVC
products.description:
The Amazon Basics 15 lb slam ball has a heavy-duty PVC shell with a sand-filled core that absorbs impact and prevents bouncing. A textured non-slip surface keeps grip during sweaty sets. It is built for slams, core strength, explosive power and conditioning.

Compared with the 6 lb rubber ball, it is far heavier and designed to be thrown at the floor rather than bounced. Against the 20 lb 2-pack, it is lighter and a single ball. The dead feel means no ricochet, which is safer in a small space.

Slam onto a hard, flat surface and not onto thin flooring. Check the seam for tears. It suits conditioning circuits and power training. For safety, keep the area clear around you and slam from chest height to the floor in front of your toes, hinging at the hips rather than rounding the back. A rubber mat under the landing spot saves the floor and cuts noise for the household below.
products.bestFor: Conditioning circuits and power training where a dead, non-bouncing ball is ideal.
cons: Not for wall throws or passes

products.name: STRPRETTY 10 lb Slam Ball, Larger Tread Design
products.description:
The STRPRETTY 10 lb slam ball has a larger tread design that increases traction and a shell that resists bouncing and rolling. It is built for strength and CrossFit-style workouts. A 10 lb weight is a sweet spot for many beginners and women who want a manageable slam ball.

Compared with the Amazon Basics 15 lb, it is lighter and easier to handle for high reps. Against the ProsourceFit slam ball, it has a larger tread pattern. The no-roll feature is handy in a small garage.

Slam on a firm floor and inspect the seams. It suits beginners and higher-rep slam circuits. A good rule is to build up reps rather than weight in the first month, so the shoulders and lower back adapt. Keep the ball dry, because sweat on the tread can make it slippery on release.
products.bestFor: Beginners and higher-rep slam circuits who want a manageable 10 lb ball.

products.name: ProsourceFit Slam Medicine Ball, Tire Tread Texture, PVC Rubber Shell
products.description:
The ProsourceFit slam ball has a supple PVC rubber shell and a non-slip tire tread surface that gives traction during intense workouts. It is a dead-weight ball that absorbs impact and holds up to slams. It is aimed at throws, slams, squats, presses and core work.

Compared with the Amazon Basics 15 lb, it offers a tread surface and a rubberized shell. Against the STRPRETTY, it has a more aggressive tire tread. The shell is built for durability under repeated impact.

Choose the weight that lets you hit full range without form breakdown. It suits conditioning enthusiasts. Wipe the tread with a damp cloth to clear chalk and dust that build up in the grooves, which keeps the traction consistent from one session to the next. Choose a weight that you can slam ten times with clean form before you move up.
products.bestFor: Conditioning enthusiasts who want a tread-textured, durable slam ball.
pros: Works for slams, squats and presses
cons: Weight choice is up to you

products.name: Amazon Basics Heavy-Duty Slam Medicine Balls, 20 lb, 2-Pack
products.description:
The Amazon Basics 20 lb slam ball 2-pack gives you two heavy PVC balls with sand-filled cores that absorb impact and prevent bouncing. A textured non-slip surface supports sweaty sessions. The pair is useful for partner workouts or carries.

Compared with the 15 lb single ball, each ball is heavier and you get two. Against the lighter slam balls, it is for stronger users. Two 20 lb balls are handy for farmer carries and partner circuits.

Start lighter if you are new to slams. It suits stronger users and gyms with a partner. Carries are a simple way to use two heavy balls: hold one against each hip or both in a bear hug and walk a few steps, building grip and core. Check the pack for even weights and give each ball a quick inspection when it arrives.
products.bestFor: Stronger users and partner workouts that need two heavy slam balls.
pros: Two 20 lb balls in one pack
Good for carries and partner work
cons: Higher tier than a single ball

buyingCriteria.explanation: A bouncing medicine ball like the Amazon Basics 6 lb rubber ball is for passes and wall throws. A slam ball like the Amazon Basics 15 lb has a dead, sand-filled core for hard slams. Using one for the other's job wears it out. If you share the ball with a partner, choose a shell that is comfortable to catch, since a hard ball hurts on a missed pass.

Rubber shells bounce and last, soft vegan leather like the Retrospec is gentle on hands, and PVC shells on slam balls resist impact. Choose by use and by how it feels in your hands. Stitching on soft shells can fray. A common beginner mistake is buying a heavy slam ball for passes, which makes the exercise sloppy and risks the lower back.

Choose a weight that lets you keep clean form for the full set. Most beginners use 6 to 10 lb for throws and 10 to 15 lb for slams. The Retrospec offers ten weights so you can progress. Weights above about 15 lb are hard to throw overhead for most people, so slam balls are the better format at that size.

A textured or tread surface keeps the ball secure with sweaty hands. The ProsourceFit has a tire tread and the STRPRETTY a large tread. A smooth shell slips. If your hands are small, test how the ball sits in your palm, because a large ball with a smooth surface is hard to control.

Heavier balls are often larger or smaller depending on design. The Amazon Basics 6 lb is 7.6 inches across. A ball that is too large is hard to grip for rotations. A ball with a dead core stays where it lands, which is useful in a small garage but means it rolls less and needs picking up.

Slams need a hard, flat surface that can take impact, and a bouncing ball needs a clear wall. Do not slam onto thin flooring. Check your space before you buy. If you plan to train outdoors, avoid wet grass and rough pavement, which scuff shells and wear off texture quickly.

cards.label: Slam ball
cards.text: The Amazon Basics 15 lb and 20 lb, the STRPRETTY and the ProsourceFit are dead-weight balls for slams. They do not bounce.

cards.label: Bouncing ball
cards.text: The Amazon Basics 6 lb rubber ball bounces for wall throws and passes. It should not be slammed hard.

howToChoose.note: Match the ball to the exercise.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A weight you can rotate with control, a textured grip and a size that fits both hands. Start light and focus on form. Keep ribs down and avoid arching the lower back during rotations.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Amazon Basics 6 lb and the Retrospec are the best fits.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You do high-rep wall balls, heavy slams every day or want commercial durability. A premium wall ball or slam ball above $50 is worth it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You train a few times a week at home. A ball under $50 is enough. Rotate between a light ball and a heavy one to keep sessions interesting.

maintenance.why: Sweat and dust degrade grip. A damp cloth keeps it clean. Dry it fully before storing.
Split seams leak sand or fill. Retire a torn ball. A small tear can grow quickly, so retire the ball early.
Thin floors crack and balls wear. Use a firm mat or concrete. A thick mat extends the life of both the ball and the floor.
Heat softens shells. Keep it in a cool place. A closet shelf is better than a hot garage.
Cracks signal wear. Replace if the shell splits. Rotate between balls if you own more than one.

faq.q: What is the difference between a slam ball and a medicine ball?
faq.a: A slam ball has a dead, sand-filled core for hard slams. A medicine ball bounces and is for passes and wall throws. Many people eventually own one of each for different parts of a workout.

faq.q: What weight should I start with?
faq.a: Most beginners start with 6 to 10 lb for throws and 10 to 15 lb for slams. Choose a weight you can control. Moving up in small steps is safer than a big jump.

faq.q: Is the price cap still valid?
faq.a: Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when the guide was updated. Check before buying. Many shoppers keep the receipt for a week in case a ball arrives damaged.

faq.q: Can I slam a bouncing medicine ball?
faq.a: Not hard. It can ricochet and wear the shell. Use a slam ball for slams. A ricochet off a hard floor can also hit you in the face.
They last with care but stitching can fray. Keep them away from rough surfaces.
Yes on a suitable floor. Use a mat to protect the floor and reduce noise. Check that the ceiling is high enough for overhead throws.
